changes.before: Implement readLimit(target). Match the worked contract and the changed-input checks without modifying the supplied input values.
changes.after: Accept a query setting only when it appears exactly once.

before: Some query settings should occur once. Silently choosing the first or last repeated value can make two layers interpret a request differently.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.
searchParams.getAll("limit") returns every occurrence as an array. length checks how many were supplied. This step checks multiplicity, not whether the text is a valid number.

Read the function call readLimit("/notes?limit=2") from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, readLimit runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
A request contains limit=2&limit=8. What does this contract return? Two values violate the exactly-one rule. Number validation is a separate step.
after: Some query settings should have one value. If a setting appears twice, different parts of a system might choose different values. This rule rejects the repeated setting instead of guessing.
searchParams holds the query settings from a URL. getAll("limit") returns an array containing every limit value, in order. An array can be empty if no limit was supplied.
values.length counts how many values were found. If the count is 1, values[0] reads that only value. Otherwise, return null to mean no single value was accepted.
This function only checks the number of occurrences. It does not check whether the text is a valid number. One supplied value can still contain invalid numeric text; that needs a separate check.
Complete readLimit(target). Return the supplied limit text only when it appears once. Return null when it is missing or repeated. Keep the original target unchanged.
